messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The flood came at night. Mei Lin was working the closing shift at the fast-food restaurant, the last one out after mopping the floors. By the time she drove home, the rain had turned the streets into rivers. She remembered the water rising past her car doors, the way the current pulled at the vehicle as she scrambled onto the roof. She remembered holding onto the radio antenna, watching her neighbor’s house slide past in the dark. What stayed with her most was not the water itself, but the sound—the low, grinding roar of debris scraping against metal, and the way the silence afterward felt heavier than any noise.

In the months that followed, Mei Lin found she could not stay asleep. She would wake at two or three in the morning, her heart pounding, certain she had heard something. She had come to believe that her emotions had been permanently damaged—that she would never feel normal again, that she no longer belonged anywhere, not even in her own home. Because she believed she could not stop bad things from happening, she began scanning her environment constantly. Every unexpected sound at work—the slam of a freezer door, the hiss of the fryer—made her flinch. She would freeze, her hand gripping the counter, waiting for disaster. She had learned that if she did not stay alert, something terrible would catch her off guard. At night, this vigilance grew worse. She checked the locks three times, then checked them again. She lay in bed listening to the house settle, certain that any creak or groan was the beginning of another catastrophe. Her husband had stopped asking why she kept the bathroom light on.

The memory of the flood did not come to her in a straight line. It arrived in fragments—the cold metal of the antenna, the smell of gasoline on the water, the sound of a dog barking somewhere in the dark. She could not piece them into a single story. When the fragments did surface, usually at work or in the middle of the night, they overwhelmed her completely. She would have to stop what she was doing, press her palms against her eyes, and wait for the wave of panic to pass. Her manager had noticed. Twice now, she had been asked to take a break. She knew the fragments were worse when she was already on edge. The more she braced herself for danger, the more the memories broke through. And the more the memories broke through, the more convinced she became that she was broken—that she could not stop this, that she would never feel safe again.

At work, the drive-through speaker crackled and spat static. Every time it popped, Mei Lin’s shoulders shot up to her ears. She had started avoiding the evening shift because the darkness outside the windows reminded her of the night of the flood. She traded hours with a coworker, taking the morning shifts even though they paid less. She told herself it was fine. She told herself she was just being careful. But she had stopped visiting her sister, who lived near the river. She had not driven past the bridge in six months. Her husband had started handling the grocery shopping. She did not explain why.

What finally brought her to the clinic was the insomnia. She had not slept more than three hours a night in two weeks. She was exhausted, but she was also terrified of what would happen if she let her guard down completely. She had come to believe that the only thing keeping her safe was her own vigilance, and that if she stopped watching, the water would find her again. She wanted to sleep, but she was certain that if she did, something bad would happen. She was not sure which frightened her more—the possibility that she was right, or the possibility that she was wrong and still could not stop.
